# Introduction 

Willow (*Lagopus lagopus*) and Rock Ptarmigan (*Lagopus muta*) are primary prey sources for the Gyrfalcon, a declining Arctic raptor species. For this research project, I aim to estimate annual ptarmigan abundance from data collected by the Peregrine Fund to support PhD student Michael Henderson's research linking adult survival of Gyrfalcons to ptarmigan numbers and other factors in Alaska along the Seward Peninsula.

## Research Question

How has ptarmigan abundance changed in the Seward Peninsula of Alaska over the last 10 years?

# Data

Since 2016, the Peregrine Fund has conducted annual distance sampling surveys along 10 mi road transects in the Seward Peninsula of Alaska. There are 15 transects, each surveyed 1-2x yearly. Surveys were completed by two observers scanning for ptarmigan in a vehicle around May each year from sunrise to noon, when ptarmigans are most active. When ptarmigan were spotted, observers tally birds and record distance to the bird with rangefinders. Data from 2016-2026 was cleaned and combined into one csv by Kara Beer. The first rows of the dataset and its dimensions are shown here:

```{r pulldata, echo = FALSE}
# set path to where you can access your data #
# Note that the path will be different for your.#
datapath <- datadir <- paste( getwd(), "/Data/", sep = "" )
# load ptarmigan raw detection data
detdf <- read.csv( file = paste( datadir, "2026-07-23_all_prey_data.csv", sep = ""),
                   header = TRUE )
#view
head( detdf ); dim( detdf )
```

## Cleaning

First, I removed all observations that are not of Rock or Willow Ptarmigan.
```{r cleannonptarm, results = 'hide'}

#database has observations that are not ptarmigan. view all the species in the species column
unique(detdf$species)

#new dataframe with only relevant columns and only for ptarmigan obs.
ptarmdetdf <- detdf %>% 
  dplyr::select(year, round, transect, observer1, observer2, species, males, females, cluster_size, distance) %>% #select relevant columns (cluster_size = ptarmigan count),
  dplyr::filter(., species == "WIPT" | species == "ROPT" )  #filter out rows that are not willow and rock ptarmigan counts

#view
head(ptarmdetdf); dim(ptarmdetdf)

```
This removes `r nrow( detdf ) - nrow(ptarmdetdf)` observations.

In my initial data exploration, I discovered that the data in the distance row was character class instead of numeric class due to the inclusion of values such as "<100," ">1200," and "U". There were also one negative distance recorded (-99). My next cleaning step is to turn the column into numeric values and filter out the negative number and the NAs converted from the greater than, less than, and U values.

```{r cleandistance, results = 'hide', warning = FALSE}

# First, check class of distance column
sapply(ptarmdetdf$distance, class)
# all character

#convert to numeric
ptarmdetdf$distance <- as.numeric(ptarmdetdf$distance)

#check again to make sure
sapply(ptarmdetdf$distance, class)
#all numeric

#drop all rows with NAs and the negative numbers
cleandetdf <- ptarmdetdf %>%
  drop_na(.,"distance") %>%
  subset(., distance >= 0)

#check for NAs
sum(is.na(cleandetdf$distance))
#0 NAs

#view
head(cleandetdf); dim(cleandetdf)

```

This removes `r nrow( ptarmdetdf ) - nrow(cleandetdf)` rows.

There are now `r nrow(cleandetdf)` observations total. There are a total of `r sum(cleandetdf$cluster_size)` individual Willow and Rock Ptarmigan counted over all 10 years, `r sum(cleandetdf$males)` of which are male and `r sum(cleandetdf$females)` of which are female. There are `r sum(wipt$cluster_size)` Willow Ptarmigan, `r sum(wipt$males)` of which are male and `r sum(wipt$females)` of which are female. There are `r sum(ropt$cluster_size)` Rock Ptarmigan, `r sum(ropt$males)` of which are male and `r sum(ropt$females)` of which are female. 

There are pretty wide disparities in numbers between species and sex, so it may be best to run 4 separate models. 

## Visualization

Key to the detection submodel of distance sampling models is fitting distance sampling curves to detection of ptarmigan by distance. I will create histograms of distance to ptarmigan for each observer pair by year for each round of surveys to look for any potential biases (are some pairs better at looking for ptarmigan than others? are observers better at finding ptarmigan close to the road than further from the road?) and to decide what kind of distance curve I should use.

First, I created a general histogram of all distances ptarmigans are detected at by species. To run the models I chose, distances will need to be binned into classes. Royle and Kery's (2016) book chapter Modeling Abundance Using Hierarchical Distance Sampling in Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology advises that bin widths be <10% of the max distance. The highest distance recorded for Willow Ptarmigan is `r max(wipt$distance)` m, 10% of which is `r max(wipt$distance)/10` m. The highest distance recorded for Rock Ptarmigan is `r max(ropt$distance)` m, 10% of which is `r max(ropt$distance)/10` m. Thus, bins of 50 m should suffice. There should be no need to truncate distances as long as distances are binned. The following histograms have distances binned by 50 m.

```{r allhist, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, results = 'hide'}

#plot histogram of distances grouped by species
ggplot( cleandetdf, aes(x = distance, fill = species)) +
  theme_classic() +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50) #bin 50 because I'm planning to bin final data by 50 m

```

So far, distance data for both species fits a half normal distribution for the distance curve. 

To start the process of visualizing data by round and observer pair, I first added a column to my dataframe with each unique pair of observers.

```{r obspair, results = 'hide'}

   last <- word(x, -1)
   tolower(paste(sort(last), collapse = "-"))
 })

#what are the unique observer pairs?
unique(cleandetdf$obsv_pair)

#check for NAs just in case
sum(is.na(cleandetdf$obsv_pair))
  
```
The unique observer pairs are: `r unique(cleandetdf$obsv_pair)`

### Round 1 Histograms by Observer Pair

Here are the histograms for round 1 of surveys for each observer pair by year to see if there are data from any pairs that should be excluded.

```{r round1hist, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, results = 'hide'}

#create an object that stores all unique observer pairs
pairs1 <- c(unique(det1$obsv_pair))
#view
#pairs1

#for loop to create histograms of distance by observer pair/year and survey (1st or 2nd)
for( p in 1:length(pairs1) ){
  # create an object with the ggplot so that you can display it 
  # in a loop 
  a <- ggplot( subset(det1, obsv_pair %in% pairs1[p]), aes(x = distance, fill = species) ) + #data subsetted to observer pair by year. plot distance and color code by species.
    theme_bw( base_size = 15 ) + #choose a preset theme
    labs( title = pairs1[p], subtitle = "Round 1" ) + #label graphs using our observer pairs
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 50) + #plot histogram
    facet_wrap(~year) #plot by survey 1 and 2
    #scale_x_discrete(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(5))
  # display your plot object
  print( a )
}
```

### Interpretation

Round 1 has more data than round 2, but both fit the half normal distribution shape well, and each distance bin has proportionally about the same count for both rounds. Unfortunately, the unmarked package does not allow for multiple replicates within seasons to be accounted for, so only using data one round may be the best way forward. From this visualization, I would consider only using round 1 data for the final model because the data is similar enough to round 2, but there is more data. 

Detection curves for observer pairs are pretty consistent with each other and most histograms fit the halfnorm function. All data can be kept, especially if I am only using round 1 data. Royle and Kery (2016) does outline a way to account for double observers in a Bayesian model, so that may be a consideration future analyses. 

## Predictors

I will not be looking at environmental covariates for the class project to keep it simple. Observers did collect environmental covariates for each survey (eg temp, wind speed), so future analysis could include them in the detection submodel to determine whether or not they influenced detection. Factors like vegetation cover and landscape features (would obscure ptarmigan, especially further out) could also influence detection, so I could consider getting these covariate values from remote sensed data, but that might be too complicated for right now. Factors like gyrfalcon and other predator abundance and vegetation data (since adults are herbivorous) could influence abundance, but ptarmigan also naturally cycle in population numbers in some areas, which could include our study area. It might be best to not include abundance covariates for now and first see how the numbers look year to year. Similar covariates could affect survival and recruitment (since this will be an open population model), but once again I will not including them for the class project for simplicity.

# Analysis

I will be running a hierarchical distance sampling (HDS) model. Unlike conventional distance sample (CDS) models, HDS models account for spatial variation in abundance between sites, since Lambda(s) measures mean site-level abundance. Total abundance in the area can still be calculated, but HDS allows us to get at the reasons for spatial variation among sites if we so choose (i.e., it's more flexible). 

I will run a multi-season HDS model with unmarked package [distsampOpen function](https://rbchan.github.io/unmarked/reference/distsampOpen.html) to account for multiple years of sampling. I may run 4 separate models (by species and sex). The general equation will be:

**N[s1] ~ Poisson (Lambda[s1])**, where N[s1] is the populations size at site s and initial sampling period t = 1. This can also be Negative Binomial or Zero-Inflated Poisson, but I will start with Poisson.

**S[st] ~ Binomial (N[st-1], phi)**, where S[st] is individuals that survive from the previous time t at site s as a function of abundance at the last time interval t-1 at site s and apparent survival probability phi.

**R[st] ~ Poisson (N[st-1], gamma)**, where R[st] is number of new recruits at site s and time t and gamma is the per capita recruitment rate.

**y[st]|N[st] ~ Multinomial (N[st], pi[st])**, where y[st] is observations at site s and time t for all distance classes conditional on abundance at site s and time t, and pi[st] is a parameter describing multinomial cell probabilities (the probability an individual occurs at site s and time t).

The general format and arguments for the code are shown below:

```{r function, eval = FALSE}

distsampOpen(lambdaformula, gammaformula, omegaformula, pformula, #abundance, recruitment, survival, detection
    data, #unmarked dataframe (unmarkedFrameDSO) with matrix of observations
    keyfun=c("halfnorm", "exp", "hazard", "uniform"), #halfnorm
    output=c("abund", "density"), unitsOut=c("ha", "kmsq"), #abundance, so don't need unitsout (which relates to density)
    mixture=c("P", "NB", "ZIP"), #P for Poisson
    K, #I think the default is max count+100 if it follows the same rules as the gdistsamp function
    dynamics=c("constant", "autoreg", "notrend", "trend", "ricker", "gompertz"), #type of pop dynamics. need to discuss
    fix=c("none", "gamma", "omega"), #omega = omega (survival) = 1, gamma = gamma (recruitment) = 0. need to discuss
    immigration=FALSE, #whether or not to include immigration term (iota) in pop dynamics
    iotaformula = ~1, #formula for average number of immigrants to a site per time step (year)
    starts, #vector of starting values
    method="BFGS", #optimization method
    se=TRUE, ...) #whether or not to calc standard errors

#my sense is to exclude all the immigration arguments for simplicity for now and bc we don't have any way to measure them
```

## Model Evaluation

I will assess model goodness-of-fit using the parametric bootstrapping function in unmarked as shown in Royle and Kery (2016): Modeling Abundance Using Multinomial N-Mixture Models. This method computes error sums-of-squares, Chi-square, and Freeman-Turkey values. I will be looking for moderate p-values for all three statistics (not close to 0 or 1). I will also compute the c-hat to test for over or under dispersion following (Johnson et al. 201: A model-based approach for making ecological inference from distance sampling data).
